newsitem.title: USA: Jury selection ends for day in Fla. tobacco case.
newsitem.headline: Jury selection ends for day in Fla. tobacco case.

text.p: Twenty-five prospective jurors were questioned on Monday in the latest case brought against the tobacco industry by attorney Norwood "Woody" Wilner, who last August dealt cigarette makers their worst loss in court in 40 years.

In a courtroom crowded with observers ranging from stock analysts to journalists to lawyers, plaintiffs' attorneys questioned potential jurors about their feelings on smoking, tobacco companies and the people who sue them.

Six jurors and three alternates will be selected to hear a wrongful death lawsuit known as Raulerson vs R.J. Reynolds, in which the sister of a smoker who died of cancer has accused the tobacco company of peddling a deadly product.
R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co is a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.

When the proceedings ended for the day, one potential juror in a pool of 53 had been dismissed and none had been seated. The woman who was dismissed said her husband had once done some work for Wilner.

The jury pool was given a list of 50 questions, among them inquiries about whether they had ever told anyone to stop smoking, had strong feelings about tobacco companies, thought the government should ban the sale of cigarettes or had a friend or relative die of lung cancer.

"Does anyone believe that a smoker has no right to sue a cigarette company?" plaintiffs' attorney Ron Motley asked 25 jurors in the first group questioned. Seven hands went up, including those of two smokers.
One woman who said smokers had no right to sue said she had switched to "light" cigarettes because they were "the lesser of two evils." She did not elaborate.

Another potential juror, a smoker, said she wanted to quit and had bought nicotine gum to help -- but had not opened it yet. A male member of the jury pool acknowledged in answer to a question that he had heard of cigarettes referred to as a "drug delivery system."
Circuit Judge Bernard Nachman said the trial was likely to last two to three weeks. Jury selection was expected to take several days and opening statements will likely begin later this week.

The proceedings mark Wilner's first tobacco trial since last August, when he won a landmark $750,000 judgment on behalf of lifelong smoker Grady Carter. The Brown & Williamson unit of B.A.T Industries has appealed the award.
In this trial, Wilner sued on behalf of Dana Raulerson, whose sister, Jean Connor, died of lung cancer at age 49. Reynolds faces possible punitive damages.
